title: Everyone Is Transforming. Nobody Is Integrating.
author: Richard Claydon
summary: Claydon's long-form Sunday Essay narrates, through the composite character of Maya — a Regional Lead in a large professional services firm — the structural problem facing leaders inside complex organisations: multiple legitimate change agendas (strategic, technological, organisational, developmental, change-management) have each been authorised independently and at different speeds, producing a combined load that no individual leader can absorb without incoherence. The essay distinguishes between transformation (buying fragments of change from separate vendors or functions) and integration (making those fragments answer to one another so the whole becomes coherent). Leaders in this environment are asked to absorb incoherence privately — to translate contradictions so others can keep moving — rather than to make incoherence visible and redesignable. Claydon identifies three levels at which integration work operates: self (noticing the leader's own pull toward rescue, contempt, or martyrdom), role (knowing what kind of legitimacy the moment requires — authorising, committing, or creating understanding), and system (seeing how Run, Serve, and Change are being arranged across the whole). The core discipline is holding all three simultaneously, accepting that 'this is not all your fault, but it is now part of your work.'
points: Organizations authorize multiple legitimate future states — strategic, technological, organizational, developmental, change-management — simultaneously and at different speeds, but do not do the integration work to make them answer to one another, then ask individual leaders to absorb the resulting incoherence.

The critical distinction Claydon draws is between absorption (working harder so the system still looks manageable, taking strain into the person) and integration (changing the relationship among the parts so the strain becomes visible, shareable, and available for redesign) — most leadership writing assumes the former while calling it the latter.

Leaders in fragmented systems must operate at three levels simultaneously — self (noticing their pull toward rescue, contempt, or martyrdom), role (knowing whether the moment requires authorising, building commitment, or creating understanding), and system (seeing where Run is overloaded, where Change is smuggled, where decision rights are performative) — and the strain begins when these levels collapse.

Effective leadership in an integration context redefines every conventional leadership task: influence becomes helping partial truths answer to one another; communication becomes making the relationship between story and load more honest; prioritisation becomes the political work of naming what will stop and what cost will no longer be hidden.

The discipline of integration work is holding two sentences simultaneously: 'This is not all your fault' (preventing shame, over-responsibility, and exhaustion) and 'It is now part of your work' (preventing the leader from becoming a commentator who sees the system but cannot act usefully within it).
quotes: In her experience, the word integration usually meant that several things had already failed to meet one another in the wild, and a group of tired people had now been assembled to admire the gap. Still, the meeting was necessary. That was the trouble. Almost everything in it was necessary.
In practice, this meant she spent a lot of her time working out which version of reality needed to be made believable to whom, by when, and at what cost to the people below the official account.

Maya wrote that phrase down, partly because it sounded important and partly because she wanted to remember it for later, when someone would inevitably be manually reconciling three spreadsheets because the frictionless intelligence had encountered a local data definition.

Absorption says: I will work harder so this still looks manageable. Integration says: let us look at what is being made manageable, by whom, and at what cost. Absorption says: I will translate the contradiction so others can keep moving. Integration says: the contradiction is data; we need to bring it into the room without letting it destroy the room.

The earlier question is: what has this system failed to integrate before asking Maya to lead? Once that is asked, the leadership work changes. Maya still has to influence the room. But influence is no longer persuasion in search of agreement. It becomes the work of helping partial truths answer to one another.

Most leadership strain begins when those levels are collapsed. The leader feels pressure and assumes it is personal. The organisation sees role difficulty and assumes it is capability. The system generates incoherence and calls it complexity.

This is not all your fault. But it is now part of your work. Not because leaders should absorb incoherence privately. Because leaders in real systems must learn how to make incoherence visible, negotiable, and redesignable.” Archived from Leadership, Rewritten (Richard Claydon, Substack) on June 19, 2026 by Tim.
